title: Stovies
subtitle: Scottish pot of potato, onion, and leftover roast meat
excerpt: A one-pot Scottish dish of potatoes and onions slowly cooked in beef dripping or butter with leftover roast beef or lamb, seasoned with salt and pepper. Traditional Monday-after-the-roast eating.
sourceNotes: F. Marian McNeill, The Scots Kitchen (1929), stovies as a traditional Scottish Monday dish made from Sunday roast leftovers. The name derives from stove, as the dish was cooked slowly on top of the stove. Found in most Scottish domestic cookery books from the nineteenth century onwards.

content.text: Stovies are a Scottish kitchen staple: potatoes and onions cooked down slowly in fat with pieces of leftover roast meat, seasoned generously and served direct from the pot. The potatoes break down at the edges as they cook and the whole dish thickens into something between a stew and a mash. It is traditionally made on Mondays from Sunday roast leftovers and needs no other accompaniment.

items.prepNote: floury variety, peeled and sliced about 1 cm thick
or leftover roast beef or lamb, roughly chopped

content.text: Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a large, heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add {{onion}} sliced onions and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until softened and beginning to colour.
Add {{beef-mince}} of beef mince or leftover roast meat if using, and stir to break up or combine. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes.
Layer {{potato}} of sliced potatoes over the onions and meat. Season well with salt and pepper at each layer.
Pour {{stock-beef}} of beef stock or water over the top. The liquid should come about halfway up the potatoes. Cover tightly with a lid.

Cook over low heat for 40 to 45 minutes, checking occasionally. The potatoes should break down at the edges and absorb most of the liquid. Shake the pan rather than stirring, to avoid breaking up the potato layers completely.
Taste, adjust the seasoning, and serve from the pot.

rows.cause: Heat too low or lid not fitted tightly
rows.fix: Make sure the lid is on firmly and the heat is set to a genuine low simmer. Waxy potatoes also take longer than floury ones.

rows.symptom: Stovies are dry and sticking to the bottom
rows.cause: Too little liquid or heat too high
rows.fix: Add a little more stock or water if it looks dry. Keep the heat on low and the lid on.
Season at every layer. Stovies need more salt than you expect, particularly if using water rather than stock.
Shake the pan rather than stirring. The potatoes should have some texture remaining alongside the broken-down edges.

content.text: Stovies are made from leftovers, cooked without fuss, and eaten with oatcakes or bread. The dish varies by region and by family. Some are dry; some are almost soupy. Some use tinned corned beef instead of roast leftovers; some skip the meat entirely. The word comes from the Scots verb stove, meaning to cook in a closed pot over low heat.
